newsitem.title: USA: Analyst sees power price gains in 4-5 years.
newsitem.headline: Analyst sees power price gains in 4-5 years.

text.p: There will be upward pressure on U.S. electricity prices once the current excess of generating capacity is absorbed in four to five years' time, Bear Stearns & Co Inc analyst Dan Scotto predicted.
Speaking to state legislators from across the country on "The Shape of the Electric Industry to Come," Scotto said, "In 10 years, we won't recognize the industries that will emerge."

But after four or five years, the forces restructuring the industry will result in price/demand dynamics that put upward prssure on power prices, Scotto said. He is Bear Stearns' Managing Director of High Grade Bonds.

If the price of power is the reason to restructure the electric utility industry, Scotto told a conference sponsored by the National Conference of State Legislators, "then everyone should be concerned." The meeting addressed "The Electric Industry in the Balance: The Legislative Role for Reform."
Power costs are a function of two "highly unstable" factors -- the cost of fuel and funds, he said.
"The luxury today is we have excess (generating) capacity in the U.S.," he said, putting it at 18 percent.
This will last four or five years, Scotto added.
If the Northeast has a hot summer this year, he said, the experience will be "a preview, a small glimpse of the instability to come."
"There are elements in place that will put an upward pressure on the prices in the future," Scotto continued.
He said equity capital will not flow to unregulated generating operations in return for an 11 percent return.

He predicted it would take a 20 percent return on equity to attract the needed funds because the "capital markets will view generating companies as highly unstable entities and will demand a premium."
However, the "wire companies," consisting of the regulated local distribution assets of present electric utilities, will be seen as "very low risk entities," he said.

They "will be allowed by the financial markets (to have) much more leverage" than present utilities, he said, predicting an average debt to equity ratio of 80 percent compare to the present 50 percent average.
Scotto also said he sees "a great consolidation in wire companies," adding there will be "a massive consolidation -- like the phone companies -- after 2005 or 2007."
